rv.q: It's a remarkable picture of restlessness and need, and reason enough to see Cullman'
If happily ever after is better than a shattered glass unicorn or getting carted off to the neighborhood loony bin, it probably shouldn’t feel less fun.
Unfortunately, even Tomei’s vivifying, staunchly committed performance isn’t enough to keep this ripe comedy at the emotional heights it needs to sustain.
A burlesque of desire, directed by Trip Cullman with desperate energy and garbled sense of time and place, it has the buoyancy of a leaky balloon that makes rude noises as it deflates.
Although the tone of the play and production waver too much to leave a permament impression, The Rose Tattoo has an interesting position in the Williams canon.
Strange, if not exactly lovely.
Allowing for Serafina’s tendency to hyperbole, she might be talking about the production in which she appears.
Instead, it’s shrill and hysterically over the top, poorly paced and blighted by some very large Italianate acting with all the authenticity of an Olive Garden chicken alfredo.
In more comic mode, Marisa Tomei gives us a passionate, sensual, and sexy Serafina Delle Rose.
Tomei adeptly navigates through passages of gravitas to find humor, and her chemistry with Elliott’s Alvaro is seductive and charming.
Tomei is a transfixing joy to spend time with; her limbs and hair are in a constant state of tossing emotion.
Unfortunately, neither direction nor casting can do much for the rest of The Rose Tattoo, which includes a bunch of supporting roles that are underbaked, overdrawn, or just plain forgettable.
Despite winning the Tony for Best Play in 1951, The Rose Tattoo still feels like one of Williams’ lesser works, missing the thunder and heat of his legendary ones.
It is wonderful enough where it really counts to overcome its mostly insignificant shortcomings.
It's a testament to the two stars that despite the production's shortcomings, they make it all worthwhile.
Stretched too broadly and the whole business can warp.
Another way of putting this is to maintain that Williams’ insistence on the play’s profundities is set aside for a production that skims the text’s surface and is content to do only that.
What it does not deserve is the pink-flamingos revival that opened Tuesday at Broadway’s Theatre, a presentation of the Roundabout Theatre Company.
This Tennessee Williams is sugar coated.
She is a light-opera soubrette cast in a role meant for a Wagnerian soprano.
What she can’t do single-handedly, though, is save us completely from Cullman’s deeply questionable directorial choices.
The Roundabout production of The Rose Tattoo is most useful in letting us understand why there have been so relatively few Broadway revivals of this play.
But sometimes the sauce just doesn't come together.

tn.cat: Best Costume Design of a Play

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this Roundabout revival, with critics praising Tomei's committed performance but faulting Trip Cullman's broad, comedic direction that misses the play's darker emotional depth.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
